sections.heading: 3 Dataset Collection and Generation
sections.text: We use the AlgoPuzzleVQA dataset introduced by Ghosal et al. (2025) , which comprises challenging visual puzzles designed to evaluate the capabilities of MLLMs in visual perception, language comprehension, and algorithmic reasoning. For our experiments, we selected nine categories from AlgoPuzzleVQA based on their suitability for conversion into text-only representations. This enables us to isolate and examine the reasoning bottlenecks of MLLMs without relying on visual inputs. The selected categories include: Clock, Checker Move, Maze, Move Box, N-Queens, Number Slide, Tower of Hanoi, Rotting Kiwi, and Water Jugs. A brief description and example for each category are provided in Appendix B . Training Data Generation: The AlgoPuzzleVQA dataset provides only 100 visual samples per category, which is insufficient for RL training. To scale up the dataset, we generated additional training samples by adapting the source code 1 1 1 https://tinyurl.com/4e5cvevv with necessary modifications. Specifically, we created 9,000 new training samples across four categories: Clock, Maze, Move Box, and N-Queens. The Clock category contains 3,000 samples, while each of the other three categories includes 2,000 samples. These samples were generated by varying features such as the clock’s shape, the color and size of the clock hands, the orientation of the grid, and the positions of the boxes and queens. The original AlgoPuzzleVQA dataset is retained as the gold test set, and we ensured that none of the generated training samples overlap with the test data. Additionally, all training examples are unique and contain no repetitions. sections.heading: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.text: In our experiments, we are going to address the following research questions. RQ1) Bottleneck of MLLMs: To what extent are the limitations of MLLMs due to challenges in visual perception or algorithmic reasoning? RQ2) Reward Function Ablation and Long Reasoning: How can different reward functions affect RL training to unlock long visual reasoning? RQ3: Generalization: How well does a RL-trained model generalize to out-of-distribution classes. Evaluation: We extract the final answer from the model’s prediction and compare it with the ground truth using exact match, reporting Accuracy as the evaluation metric Toh et al. (2025) . Prior work by Ghosal et al. (2025) evaluated model performance in both multiple-choice (MCQ) and open-ended settings. In our preliminary experiments, we found that in the MCQ setting, models often guessed the correct answer from the provided options, even when their reasoning was incorrect. This limits the evaluation’s ability to accurately reflect the model’s true capabilities. Therefore, we evaluate all models exclusively in the open-ended setting, where no answer options are provided. We recommend that future work adopt the open-ended format to accurately assess models’ performance.

sections.heading: 4.1 Bottleneck Experiments
sections.text: To analyze the reasoning bottlenecks, we evaluate Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Claude-3.7-Sonnet in thinking mode across the nine selected categories. We conduct the experiments in two settings: i) Multimodal ( <image, question> ): where the image and corresponding question are provided to the model, ii) Text-only ( <text-representing image, question> ): where the image is converted into a text description, which is then passed to the model along with the question. For instance, in the ‘Checker-Move’ category, text descriptions are simple strings where colors are encoded as characters—‘R’ for red, ‘G’ for green, and ‘-’ for white space. Other categories follow similarly intuitive character-based representations. Examples of how images are converted into character-based textual representations are provided in Table 7 . We use a unified prompt structure across both settings, illustrated in Figure 2 . Figure 2: Generic prompt structure used across all categories in both multimodal and text-only settings. In the text-only setting, the image is replaced with its textual representation so that the entire input is in text.

sections.heading: 4.2 Training Settings
sections.text: We use the Qwen-2.5-VL-7B (instruct) model for our experiments, selected for its strong visual reasoning capabilities among open-source multimodal models Yang et al. (2024) . We train the model using the GRPO DeepSeek-AI (2025) , a reinforcement learning–based optimization method, with synthetically generated training samples (Section 3 ). Building on this setup, we examine how reinforcement learning may influence the model’s reasoning behavior by constructing two datasets, each aligned with a complementary hypothesis. First, we hypothesize that training on challenging, high-difficulty samples can help unlock the model’s longer reasoning abilities. Since Clock is one of the categories where the base model struggles most, we construct a training set consisting of 3,000 samples exclusively from this category, referred to as Clock-3k . Second, we hypothesize that exposure to a diverse set of reasoning categories during RL training could encourage the model to make more generalizable and transferable improvements in reasoning. To test this, we create a second training set, Diverse-8k , comprising 8,000 samples distributed evenly across four categories: Clock, Maze, Move-Box, and N-Queens. Further details on training settings and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix A . sections.heading: 5.1 Bottleneck of MLLMs
sections.text: Table 3 presents the performance of Claude-3.5 and Claude-3.7 across different categories in both the multimodal and text-only settings. We observe a substantial performance gain when the image is replaced with its textual description, indicating that the models struggle more with visual perception than with algorithmic reasoning. On average, Claude-3.5 improves by 26.7 percentage points and Claude-3.7 by 23.6 points in the text-only setting. The improvement is especially striking in categories like Clock , where Claude-3.7’s accuracy jumps from 7% to 83%, and N-Queens , where both models achieve near-perfect accuracy once the visual input is replaced by structured text. These results empirically validate that visual perception is the primary bottleneck in MLLMs for solving these reasoning puzzles. To further support this, we conducted a qualitative analysis and observed that initial errors often originate from incorrect visual perception, which then propagates through the reasoning chain. For example, in the Clock category, models often fail to read the time from the positions of the clock hands; in N-Queens , they struggle to correctly identify the queens’ positions on the board; and in Move Box , they fail to recognize the spatial positions of the person, box, and target flags. Table 8 presents a few representative examples where failures in visual reasoning lead to incorrect model predictions. Figure 3: An example comparing reasoning between the base (Qwen-2.5-VL-7B) and RL-trained versions with different reward strategies. With the Mixture reward, the model generates grounded, multi-step visual reasoning–accurately describing fine-grained image details such as the distinct colors of the hour and minute hands. Notably, this structured long-form reasoning emerges naturally from RL training (see Figures 14 and 15 for additional examples). The model also performs step-by-step self-evaluation, revisiting and verifying each reasoning step before concluding with its final answer.

sections.heading: 5.2 Reward Function Ablation and Long Reasoning
sections.text: Overall performance improves with diverse data: As illustrated in Table 2 , training with the diverse dataset yields improvements across all reward functions compared to training solely on hard samples (Clock-3k). The proposed mixture reward achieves the highest average score (15.56), followed closely by the only-accuracy reward (15.11). Interestingly, the no-accuracy reward produces unexpected behavior: in both settings, it surpasses the baseline, and in the Clock-3k setting, it outperforms several other reward functions. These findings are consistent with Shao et al. (2025) , which reports that RL training without a verifiable reward signal can still improve performance. Nevertheless, certain categories remain challenging: the model consistently struggles with Clock and Tower of Hanoi tasks, in line with Fu et al. (2025) , showing that these puzzles are intrinsically difficult due to abstract temporal and recursive reasoning demands. Mixture reward unlocks long reasoning capability in MLLMs: Our reward function design incentivizes the emergence of long visual reasoning in the model. Under the vanilla and no-accuracy rewards, the model produces minimal intermediate reasoning, often jumping directly to the answer with little explanation of the image. Our objective was to encourage multistep, long-structured reasoning grounded in visual information, with the expectation that this would improve performance. Both the mixture and continuous rewards achieve this goal. As shown in Figure 3 , the model generates structured reasoning steps that reference and explain different parts of the image—exhibiting the ‘think with image’ phenomenon Zheng et al. (2025b) ; Fan et al. (2025b) . Notably, this behavior emerges across both in-domain and out-of-domain categories, indicating that our reward design and training strategy successfully unlock MLLMs’ long reasoning capability. Interestingly, the Only-Accuracy reward’s performance is on par with or better than the mixture reward in about half of the classes, especially in out-of-domain settings. This suggests that long reasoning alone does not guarantee improved accuracy for MLLMs Shao et al. (2025) .

To evaluate generalization, we measure performance on both in-domain (seen) and out-of-domain (unseen) classes. As shown in Table 4 , training on a single-category dataset (Clock-3k) results in limited generalization. In contrast, the Diverse-8k dataset substantially improves performance across nearly all classes, outperforming the baselines in both in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) settings. We observe a trade-off between ID and OOD performance: higher ID accuracy often comes at the expense of OOD generalization, likely due to overfitting during RL training. Nevertheless, OOD performance with RL consistently exceeds the no-RL baseline. Notable, the model demonstrates emergent reasoning capabilities across both in-domain and out-of-domain categories (Figures 14 and 15 ). Performance varies significantly across classes: To further investigate generalization, we explore the best-performing reward function for each category with the model trained on the Diverse-8K dataset. Detailed class-specific results are provided in Figure 4 . No single reward function consistently dominates across all classes; some reward functions excel in certain categories but underperform in others. Five different reward functions achieved the maximum score in different categories. For the number slide class, performance dropped with RL training. This variability highlights the heterogeneity in task difficulty and model behavior. Figure 4: Performance comparison across categories showing baseline vs. maximum scores and improvement margins. Reward functions that achieved the maximum score are indicated below each category. Results are reported for models trained on the Diverse-8K dataset.

sections.heading: 5.4 Error Analysis
sections.text: Despite being our best-performing model, the RL-trained Qwen-7B achieves only 15.56% accuracy. To understand this limited performance, we qualitatively analyze the errors and identify four primary causes of failure. First, the model makes visual understanding errors—even after generating extensive visual reasoning, it incorrectly identifies object positions or attributes in the input image. See the generated completion with the mixture reward in figure 3 . Second, the model also fails at algorithmic reasoning, generating erroneous intermediate computations or decision steps. Miscalculation of time ….<intermediate reasoning>…. Subtract the Time: Start with the hours. Subtracting 2 hours from 1 o’clock results in 9 o’clock. ….<continue reasoning>…. Third, we observe inconsistencies in which the model’s final answer contradicts its prior reasoning. Contradiction with own reasoning ….<intermediate reasoning>…. Therefore, the time is confidently determined to be 12:35 . <answer> 12.37 <answer> Finally, for a small number of cases, the model fails to produce a valid answer, continuing to generate tokens without reaching a definitive conclusion. Continue generation without answer ….<intermediate reasoning>…. The hour hand is closest to the 1. The hour hand is not aligned with the 11 ….<continue reasoning>…. Do not generate any <answer> tag. Overall, the error analysis highlights the multifaceted challenges posed by visual puzzle tasks. Our findings suggest that, beyond encouraging extended reasoning, this task may require reward signals that explicitly incentivize accurate visual grounding—for example, evaluating the intermediate reasoning with a strong LLM-based judge. Incorporating such signals represents a promising direction for future research.

sections.heading: 6 Related Work
sections.text: Recently, research on examining visual reasoning abilities of MLLMs has increased significantly Chen et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2024) . Several benchmarks have been introduced to evaluate these capabilities, including abstract visual puzzles Song et al. (2025) , diagrammatic and symbolic reasoning tasks Li et al. (2025a) , and algorithmic visual reasoning Ghosal et al. (2025) . Across these settings, MLLMs consistently struggle to uncover the visual relations necessary for correct inference. Although CoT prompting has proven effective for eliciting reasoning in text-only domains Wei et al. (2022) ; Kojima et al. (2022) , extensions of CoT-like reasoning to visual inputs show that models frequently generate interpretations that are weakly grounded in the image Dong et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2025a) ; Zhang et al. (2024) . Existing studies typically evaluate models based solely on prediction accuracy, providing limited insight into whether errors stem from visual misinterpretation or from incorrect algorithmic reasoning Ghosal et al. (2025) ; Bi et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2024) . In this work, we perform a systematic inspection to isolate the source of error. Specifically, we substitute images with textual descriptions across diverse puzzle categories, enabling a controlled comparison that provides causal evidence that visual perception is the primary bottleneck in visual reasoning. Reinforcement Learning has recently emerged as a way to improve reasoning in MLLMs. This is primarily motivated by the advances in process supervision and verifiable reward modeling from text-only systems Lightman et al. (2023) ; DeepSeek-AI (2025) . In the visual setting, these ideas are adapted by using reward signals that verify whether intermediate reasoning steps are consistent with the image. For instance, vision-language process reward models Wang et al. (2025b) ; Ong et al. (2025) provide feedback on reasoning steps by checking them against visual evidence. In parallel, some studies explore multimodal extensions of R1-style training to elicit longer reasoning trajectories for diagrams, mathematical problems, and synthetic visual tasks Yang et al. (2025b) ; Shen et al. (2025) ; Zhou et al. (2025) . Complementary approaches such as GRIT Fan et al. (2025a) and DeepEyes Zheng et al. (2025c) incorporate explicit visual grounding, encouraging models to reference image regions during multi-step explanations. However, these approaches rely on some form of intermediate supervision such as tool calling, executable tool outputs, bounding boxes, or annotated reasoning traces. As a result, they do not address settings in which structured supervision is difficult to obtain, such as visual puzzles. An open question remains as to whether long, structured reasoning can be induced purely through reward design. In this work, we take a step toward addressing this gap by designing reward functions and systematically evaluating their impact on encouraging long, structured visual reasoning without requiring additional supervision beyond reward evaluation itself.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our primary objective was to investigate whether reward-based RL fine-tuning can encourage models to perform long, multi-step visual reasoning required to solve complex puzzles. While alternative approaches such as SFT could potentially boost performance on a specific dataset, they cannot guide a model to exhibit step-by-step reasoning behavior. Another possibility could have been SFT with explicit reasoning traces. However, for visual puzzle datasets, collecting high-quality chain-of-thought annotations is extremely challenging and costly, mainly because the reasoning is often multi-hop, brittle, and domain-specific. For these reasons, we focus on reward-driven RL fine-tuning, where the aim was not merely to fit the dataset but to induce emergent long-horizon reasoning behavior, which we believe is better aligned with the nature of visual puzzle solving.
